lesson.child_mission: Pollination moves pollen to the part of a flower that can lead to seed formation; insects, wind or other animals can be pollinators.
lesson.evidence_instructions: Save the independent response, specific revisions and both short-answer explanations; record oral evidence for speaking tasks.
lesson.extension: Apply the same science idea to a new object or material, then compare two pieces of evidence for strength.
lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Explain why a flowering plant in a sealed room with no insects or airflow might make fewer seeds.

FEEDBACK
Less pollination → fewer fertilised flowers → fewer seeds (simplified Year 4 model).

WATCH FOR
Calling the flower “just pretty” misses its role in reproduction.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Label a flower diagram (pollen, petals, where seeds may form). Write a pollination story for an insect and for wind. List two ways gardens support pollinators.

Write a short reflection naming one observation or step you corrected and why.
lesson.learning_intention: Pollination moves pollen to the part of a flower that can lead to seed formation; insects, wind or other animals can be pollinators.
materials: Optional: safe everyday objects for observation
lesson.offline_alternative: Use paper and pencil to complete the original task, then retain a photograph or short parent observation as evidence.
lesson.parent_notes:
Parent: Marking guidance for the independent task: Label a flower diagram (pollen, petals, where seeds may form). Write a pollination story for an insect and for wind. List two ways gardens support pollinators. Accept equivalent original responses that show the same skill.

Parent: Written model 1: Original response on new material: Less pollination → fewer fertilised flowers → fewer seeds (simplified Year 4 model). Reasoning: I used pollination by attending to pollen rather than copying the worked model.

Parent: Written model 2: Common error: Calling the flower “just pretty” misses its role in reproduction. Correction: Less pollination → fewer fertilised flowers → fewer seeds (simplified Year 4 model). Why: the correction restores accurate use of pollination.

Parent: Likely misconception: Calling the flower “just pretty” misses its role in reproduction. Keep sample answers out of the child role.

Parent: Short-answer focus 1: Investigate or describe a fresh example (not the worked objects) that uses pollination. Record evidence and explain how it supports your claim.

Parent: Short-answer focus 2: Name one science misconception about pollination, correct it with evidence, and say why the correction works.

Parent: Marking notes: Require a new example, named observations and a claim–evidence link. / Require misconception + corrected claim + evidence reason..

teach_steps.example:
WORKED MODEL
Bee visits flower → pollen sticks → bee visits another flower → pollen transfer. Wind can shake pollen between grass flowers. After successful pollination, seeds can develop.

TRY FIRST
Explain why a flowering plant in a sealed room with no insects or airflow might make fewer seeds.

FEEDBACK
Less pollination → fewer fertilised flowers → fewer seeds (simplified Year 4 model).
teach_steps.explain:
Pollination moves pollen to the part of a flower that can lead to seed formation; insects, wind or other animals can be pollinators.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner base claims on observation, fair tests and design evidence, rather than guessing from a picture alone. Keep every claim linked to what was seen or measured.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the observations, properties or test steps that carry the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Compare your record with the feedback: did you use the same skill and show your evidence? If a result is uncertain, identify what would have to be observed or tested again. One deliberate, evidence-based revision is more useful than writing a longer answer.
